nameStory: Sweet Annie gets her friendly name from her distinctively sweet, almost fruity fragrance that's released when you crush the leaves. Unlike many of her bitter relatives in the wormwood family, this plant has a pleasant, aromatic scent that some describe as reminiscent of sweet herbs or even bubble gum. The 'Annie' part likely comes from 'annual,' since this wormwood completes its entire life cycle in just one year.
description: Sweet Annie is a tall, feathery annual herb that can reach 3-6 feet in height by late summer. It has a distinctive Christmas tree-like silhouette with finely divided, lacy leaves that create an airy, delicate appearance. The plant produces tiny yellowish-green flower heads in dense, branching clusters at the top, but the flowers are so small they're barely noticeable. What really sets this plant apart is its sweet, pleasant fragrance when the leaves are crushed.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Crush a leaf and smell it - the sweet, fruity fragrance is unmistakable and unlike any other wormwood. The leaves are deeply divided into threadlike segments, giving them a feathery, fern-like appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in a distinctive Christmas tree shape, tall and narrow with the main stem clearly visible and side branches getting shorter toward the top. The whole plant has an airy, delicate look despite its height.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellowish-green flower heads, each only about 1/8 inch across, arranged in dense branching clusters. The flowers are so small you might miss them - they look more like tiny green beads than typical daisy-family flowers.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Smooth, green to reddish stems that are relatively thin for the plant's height. The stems have a clean, hairless appearance and often develop reddish coloring, especially toward the base.

habitat: Sweet Annie thrives in disturbed soils and waste places, often appearing along roadsides, in vacant lots, and at field edges throughout New England. It prefers full sun and well-drained soils, and has a knack for colonizing areas where the ground has been recently disturbed. You'll sometimes find it growing with other weedy species like ragweed and goldenrod in abandoned agricultural areas.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring, producing small rosettes of finely divided leaves. Young plants are only a few inches tall but already have the characteristic sweet fragrance when crushed.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly, reaching their full height of 3-6 feet by mid to late summer. The distinctive Christmas tree shape becomes apparent, and the sweet fragrance intensifies as the plant matures.
seasonality.fall: Tiny yellowish-green flowers bloom in late summer through early fall in dense clusters at branch tips. Seeds develop quickly after flowering, and plants begin to turn brown and dry out.
seasonality.winter: Dead brown stalks may persist through winter, standing like dried Christmas trees in the landscape. The plant is annual, so only dried stems and scattered seeds remain until spring germination.

funFact: This humble roadside weed contains artemisinin, a compound that won the 2015 Nobel Prize in Medicine for its ability to treat malaria - one of the most important antimalarial drugs in the world comes from a plant you might walk past every day in New England!
confusionNotes: Sweet Annie is most easily confused with other wormwoods, but the sweet fragrance test is foolproof - all other wormwoods smell bitter or unpleasant when crushed. Common mugwort grows taller and has broader leaf segments, while the exotic absinthe wormwood has silvery-gray foliage instead of bright green.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'wormwood,' Sweet Annie actually smells pleasant unlike its bitter relatives. The plant is native to Asia but has naturalized in scattered locations across North America. It's still relatively uncommon in New England compared to other wormwoods, making each sighting somewhat special.
compareHints: Among New England's wormwoods, Sweet Annie is unique for its sweet fragrance and annual growth habit - most other wormwoods are perennial and smell bitter. It's also taller and more delicate-looking than common mugwort, lacks the silvery leaves of hoary mugwort, and has a much more pleasant scent than the notoriously bitter absinthe wormwood.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Artemisia species, common mugwort is the tallest and most common, with the most deeply divided leaves.
Unlike common mugwort which has green leaves with white undersides, hoary mugwort is silvery-white all over and much more compact.
Among New England's Artemisia species, field sagewort stands out for its preference for the driest, sandiest soils and its exceptionally finely-divided silvery leaves.

Silver wormwood stands out from its New England Artemisia relatives by its intensely silvery-white appearance - common mugwort has green tops to its leaves, while hoary mugwort is more coastal and has different leaf shapes.
Absinthe wormwood is much more silvery and aromatic than common mugwort, which has green leaves with white undersides.
Among New England's Artemisia species, biennial wormwood has the most finely divided leaves - much more delicate-looking than the broader-lobed common mugwort or the silvery hoary mugwort.
